work_order.confidence_rationale: Every finding was re-checked against main at f2aab6c rather than taken from the issue text. Six reproduce exactly as written, one (the cascade override) I confirmed by running QA's append against a prototype resolver, and one (the coordinated-rename contradiction) is a defect in a merged artifact I cannot edit, so the fix choice is mine and is argued in approach. The confidence is not higher because the cascade guard introduces a small CSS resolver into the test suite: its vocabulary has to be pinned by its own cases or it becomes a new false-pass surface, and the implementer can still get a selector form subtly wrong.
work_order.understanding:
#51 landed three tests that pin the page h1 to its .page-title stylesheet rule, so AC-2 ('the page title renders at 22.4px with no top margin') is machine-checkable. This ticket closes the eight holes in that guard, all of which I re-verified on main.

Six come from the review of #54 and two from QA on it, and after deduplication they are five defects, not eight:

1. The class-attribute extractor is /\bclass="([^"]*)"/. A word boundary matches inside data-class=, so <h1 data-class="page-title"> satisfies it: the suite is green while no class attribute exists in the markup and the heading falls back to the UA default. The issue proposes /<h1\s[^>]*\bclass="([^"]*)"/ as the fix. That does not fix it — [^>]* consumes the 'data-' and \b is a boundary between '-' and 'c', so it matches the same false shape. I ran both against the string; both return 'page-title'. The fix is to anchor on whitespace: /\sclass="([^"]*)"/, which returns undefined for data-class= and still matches the class in either attribute order.

2. The pinning test finds its anchor with .find() over the file's own lines, and its own line 971 contains the anchor literal, so deleting the real call site at line 135 makes .find() return the search line. The test still fails, but on the wrong assertion.

3. The class-to-markup and class-to-stylesheet links are held by two independent literals, and three statements in #51's work order (approach §3, out_of_scope[2], risks[0]) say a coordinated rename of page-title passes on purpose. It does not: renaming both sides to .pageHeading gives 2 failures. The reviewer offers two fixes and says not to do both. The 'correct the work order' half of that choice is not available here — #51 is merged and its work-order.json is a historical artifact no ticket can edit — so the code half is the only one that can be taken, and I take it: read the class off the rendered h1 and resolve the stylesheet rule dynamically, keeping the three literal declarations.

4. A later, higher-specificity h1 rule overrides .page-title with the suite fully green. Appending '#main h1 { font-size: 2.4rem; line-height: 1.6; margin-top: 24px; }' leaves every .page-title declaration intact, node --test reports 271 pass / 0 fail, and the heading then computes 38.4px in the browser. The existing test pins declarations as text, which cannot see the cascade, and no test in the suite reads a computed style. This is the only finding here that is a live hole in shipped behaviour rather than a hole in a guard.

5. The fileURLToPath import at line 7 exists only to wrap import.meta.url for readFileSync, twenty lines before a test that uses the URL form directly.

6. The test file's comment declares a deliberate exception to .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md ('class names are styling hooks, not assertions'), but that memory file cannot be edited by any ticket and does not mention the exception. Not fixable in code; named in out_of_scope with the note the Librarian needs.
work_order.root_cause:
Every finding is one of two root causes, and neither is in the production code — src/web/pages.js:56 and src/web/styles.css:137 are correct as shipped and this ticket changes neither.

The first is that the guard pins strings instead of the thing the string stands for. The class name was hard-coded at both ends of a link that is supposed to be held by a check, the search for the production call site matched the search itself, and the class attribute was located by a pattern loose enough to match a different attribute. Each is a literal standing in for a fact.

The second is that a declaration is not a rendering. The stylesheet test asserts three declarations exist on .page-title; CSS decides what a browser applies by cascade, so a rule that outranks it — higher specificity, or equal and later, including inside a @media block — leaves every assertion satisfied and the heading wrong. Nothing in the suite can observe the result, because a computed style needs a browser and this suite is node:test with no DOM.
work_order.approach:
Test-only, confined to test/web/pages.test.js. No production file changes: the emitted markup and the stylesheet rule are both correct today, and the shipped behaviour of #51 is safer than the intent its work order described, so this ticket keeps it and fixes the prose-shaped holes in the guard. §1 — Drop the unnecessary import. Delete line 7 ('import { fileURLToPath } from "node:url"') and write line 970 as readFileSync(import.meta.url, 'utf8'). The URL form is what line 992 already uses and what test/ops/ready-script.test.js:5 uses with no fileURLToPath anywhere, so the whole file ends on one idiom. §2 — One shared extractor, anchored on whitespace. Add a file-local helper above the pinning tests: function pageTitleClass(html) { const h1 = /]*>/.exec(html)?.[0] ?? ''; assert.match(h1, /data-testid="page-title"/, 'the page h1 is the hook under test'); return /\sclass="([^"]*)"/.exec(h1)?.[1] ?? ''; } The leading \s is the whole point and the comment above it must say so: \bclass= also matches inside data-class=, which is the false pass this ticket exists to close, and the reviewer's proposed /]*\bclass="([^"]*)"/ does too. Both ends of the link read the class through this one helper, which is what makes it a check rather than two literals that happen to agree. §3 — Test at line 981 ('the shipped page h1 carries the styling class the stylesheet rules on') keeps its render and its testid assertion, then replaces the line 985 assertion with: the extracted class is a non-empty plain identifier (/^[A-Za-z_-][A-Za-z0-9_-]*$/ — a class with regex metacharacters cannot be escaped into the stylesheet lookup below, so fail loudly rather than build a pattern that could match the wrong rule), and a rule for that exact class exists in src/web/styles.css. Add two cases to this test: assert.doesNotMatch on '

Command dashboard

' fed to pageTitleClass, named 'a data-class attribute is not a class attribute'; and assert.equal(pageTitleClass('

x

'), '', 'a missing class attribute yields no class, not a false one'). The first is the regression for the finding this ticket opens with; the second pins that the extractor degrades to '' instead of undefined. §4 — Test at line 991 ('the .page-title rule still carries the declarations the page title depends on') becomes async and resolves its selector dynamically: render '/' with freshRepos(), take pageTitleClass(html), then new RegExp(`\\.${cls}\\s*\\{([^}]*)\\}`) against the stylesheet. The three declaration assertions (margin: 0, font-size: 1.4rem, line-height: 1.25) stay literal and unchanged — AC-5 is about the declarations, not the name, and pinning them is what keeps the coordinated rename cheap. The rule-name assertion message must name the class the h1 actually carries so a one-sided rename says which end moved. Rename the test to 'the rule the page h1 carries still holds the declarations the page title depends on'. §5 — Add a cascade test after it, and this is the real work. 'nothing outranks the page title rule for the typography the h1 depends on'. It reads src/web/styles.css, strips comments, and for each of font-size, line-height and the margin-top bucket (margin, margin-top, margin-block, margin-block-start) works out which rule the browser would actually apply to

and asserts the winner is the class rule. - Candidate selection. A selector branch can reach the page h1 if it contains h1 as a type token anywhere, or its last compound carries the page-title class, or its last compound is *, html or body (those reach the h1 by inheritance, and being generous here can only produce a failure, never a pass). Split comma lists into branches first; evaluate each. A branch that cannot reach the h1 is skipped without being parsed, so an exotic selector elsewhere in the file — .checklist li:not(.x) — is ignored and never breaks the suite. Skip at-rules and keyframe selectors (a selector starting with @, or 0% / 100% / from / to). - Specificity. Count #id (a), .class, [attr] and single-colon pseudo-classes (b), and bare type names (c) over the branch; * counts as nothing. Rules in a @media or @supports block are evaluated as ordinary candidates — a responsive override of the h1's font-size is a real override at narrow widths and the failure message must name the at-rule condition so the reader knows when it bites. - A candidate outranks the class rule when (a, b, c) is greater, or equal and the candidate is declared later in the file. For each outranking declaration of a property in scope, fail with a message naming the branch, the property and the class rule's winning value. Note that a later '* { font-size: 2.4rem }' does NOT fail: the class still wins at (0,1,0) and the h1 is unaffected, so failing there would be a false alarm. The existing reset at line 25 and the body typography at line 31 must both pass, which is the check that the resolver is not simply flagging everything. - Unsupported syntax throws. Supported: id, class, attribute, single-colon pseudo-class, type, *, comma lists, descendant and '>' combinators. Anything else — a pseudo-element, '+', '~', a functional pseudo-class such as :not(…) — throws an Error naming the offending selector, so an unparseable stylesheet fails the suite loudly instead of passing for the wrong reason. Only candidate branches are parsed, so this cannot fire on unrelated CSS. I wrote and ran this resolver against the real stylesheet before planning: clean tree green, QA's appended '#main h1 { font-size: 2.4rem; line-height: 1.6; margin-top: 24px; }' red on all three properties, the same rule inside '@media (max-width: 900px)' red, the same rule moved above .page-title red on specificity, a coordinated rename to .pageHeading green, a later '* { font-size: 2.4rem }' green, and '.checklist li:not(.x)' ignored without throwing. Follow that shape; the differences between it and your implementation are where the bug would be. Pin the resolver itself in the same test — it is a test helper making a claim about CSS, and an unpinned one is a new false pass: '#main h1' beats '.page-title', '.a.b' beats '.a', '*' beats nothing, a '>' combinator is not a type name, and ':not(' throws rather than parsing to zero. §6 — The call-site pinning test at line 969. Delete the 'import { fileURLToPath }' dependency per §1, build the needle from parts so the search line cannot match itself — 'the h1 carries the page-title' + ' hook' — and add one assertion that the needle occurs exactly once in the file: assert.equal(source.split('\n').filter((line) => line.includes(needle)).length, 1, 'the anchor is found exactly once'). That is what turns the finding from diagnosability into a real pin: with the needle un-splittable, deleting the production call site makes .find() return undefined and the existing assert.ok(callSite, 'the 25-shell h1 assertion is still in this file') fires on itself, which is the message the reader needs. §7 — Rewrite the comment at lines 977-980. It currently says the assertion is a deliberate exception to .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md, which is true, and the file that would record it cannot be edited by this pipeline. Say that in the comment: the exception is deliberate, the class name is the single hook that reaches the stylesheet rule, and .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md is owned by the Librarian and does not yet record the exception — so the next agent who reads that file should not read this test as a convention violation or delete it as redundant. After all of this the literal 'page-title' appears in the test file only inside the H1_HOOK matcher comment and the shipped-markup sample strings at lines 146-152, which pin the behavioural testid, not the class.

risks: The cascade resolver is a test helper that makes a claim about CSS, and an unpinned one is a new false-pass surface — the same failure mode this ticket was filed for. It is mitigated by throwing on unsupported syntax rather than guessing, and by pinning its own specificity cases, but a selector form it reads wrongly (a pseudo-class counted as a type, a compound mis-split) would be a silent hole. Treat any change to its vocabulary as a change to a guard.

A legitimate responsive override of the page title inside a @media block now fails the suite. That is intended — a narrow-width font-size on the h1 makes AC-1 false at that width — but it means a future responsive-typography ticket has to change this guard deliberately rather than discover it as a surprise failure. The failure message names the at-rule condition so the reader knows when it bites.

The guard fails on declarations, not on the rendered heading. A stylesheet whose cascade this resolver mis-models could still render differently from what the test claims. The browser acceptance criteria AC-1 and AC-6 are the only thing in this pipeline that observes the real result, and they are checked once per run rather than per commit.

Deleting the .page-title literal from the tests means no unit test pins the class name any more. A one-sided rename still fails loudly (no rule, or no such class), but the failure arrives one stage later than it did under the literals. That is the behaviour #51's work order said it wanted and its delivered tests did not have.

The class-name assertion remains a deliberate exception to .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md, which says class names are styling hooks and not assertions. That file is reserved for the Librarian and no ticket can edit it, so the exception continues to live only in a comment in the file it constrains — the reviewer's point, not fixable here. It is named in out_of_scope so it is on the record rather than only in a comment.

None of these changes send the app anywhere new. env.api_allowlist in .sdlc/config.yml (localhost:* and 127.0.0.1:*) is unchanged and the diff adds no fetch, no form and no client-side data flow, so QA is not blocked on an allowlist entry.
out_of_scope: Recording the class-name exception in .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md. .sdlc/memory/** is reserved for the Librarian and the reserved-path guard refuses any ticket that touches it — the reviewer said so and was right. This ticket cannot carry it. What it can do, and does, is make the comment in test/web/pages.test.js say explicitly that the exception is deliberate and that the memory file does not yet record it, so the next agent who reads the memory file does not delete the pin as redundant. The Librarian's note belongs on issue #51, which is where the reviewer asked for it.

Correcting #51's work-order.json. Its approach §3, out_of_scope[2] and risks[0] all say a coordinated rename of the class passes, and the delivered tests did not permit one. That file is a merged historical artifact that no ticket edits, so the contradiction can only be resolved in the code — which is what approach §4 does, adopting the reviewer's option (a) and not option (b). Option (b) was not taken silently: it is the reviewer's second choice and was unavailable, and taking (a) is what makes #51's stated intent true rather than a note in a dead file.

Making the cascade check a rendered-value check in CI. A computed style needs a browser, this suite is node:test with no DOM, and the project has no headless-browser harness; adding Playwright or jsdom would be a new runtime dependency for one assertion, against conventions.md's stdlib-first rule. QA checks the real value in a browser on every run (AC-1), which is the project's existing answer to this and does not change here.

The 25-shell behavioural h1 test and the H1_HOOK matcher from #46. Both are deliberate: the hook is pinned on the testid so a CSS rename cannot fail a behavioural test, and the matcher is relaxed on purpose with its own pinning test at lines 145-152. This ticket changes the extractor used by the class-name assertion only; H1_HOOK stays exactly as it is.

Generalising the cascade resolver into a shared CSS library or a src/ module. It exists to check one heading on one page. A general cascade engine has one caller and would be the abstraction this repo's conventions warn against.
evidence: Issue #55 opens with the false pass; confirmed on main at f2aab6c. The whitespace-anchored /\sclass="([^"]*)"/ returns undefined on that input and 'page-title' on both '<h1 class="page-title" ...>' and '<h1 data-testid="page-title" class="page-title">', so it keeps the attribute-order tolerance #46 bought.

review.title: The comment above mayReachPageTitle states an invariant the function does not hold, in the one direction that matters. Lines 1183-1186 read: 'Every branch that may reach the h1 is then re-checked exactly by parseSelector below — so being generous here can only produce a failure or a throw, never a false pass.' The function is generous about '*'/html/body and stingy about the class-in-attribute form: the last line is `return last.includes('.' + cls)`, so a branch whose only class reference is '[class~="page-title"]' or '[data-testid="page-title"]' is dropped and never re-checked by anything. The comment is not a neutral description that has drifted; it is the argument a maintainer would rely on to decide that editing this function is safe, and it is false. A guard that documents its own safety property wrongly is worse than one that documents nothing, because the wrong comment reads as a reviewed conclusion. The immediately following comment (1193-1198) has the mirror problem: it narrates h1[data-testid], h1:hover, h1:first-child and main > h1[data-testid] being 'all dropped here, never reached parseSelector, and never reported', which describes a hole this same PR closed four lines later — shipped code carrying a bug report about a bug it no longer has, with no version anchor to tell the reader which state he is looking at.

review.title: The cascade guard is ~270 lines of a CSS specificity engine living in a test file, with exactly one caller and one assertion, and its own cost is now measurable rather than hypothetical. PAGE_TITLE_PROPERTIES through outrankingPageTitleDeclarations (1160-1430) is a selector splitter, a selector parser, a specificity comparator, a stylesheet flattener, a declaration parser, a branch splitter and a cascade comparator — re-implementing a language the test file is now the maintainer of, for a single question ('does anything beat .page-title for these three properties'). The work order weighed this and chose specificity over the ~10-line source-order alternative, and I think that call is right on its own terms; AC-2's repro is a higher-specificity rule, which source order alone does not catch. But the justification offered in approach §5 and risks[0] is that the resolver is pinned and throws rather than guesses, and in the delivered file one of the four functions is unpinned (the finding above) and the two holes reviewer A reproduced both live inside it. A guard of this size is only worth its size if the pin is complete, and today it is not. Read at 3am this is 270 lines to answer a question a browser already answers, sitting in a test file that now has a CSS parser in it — and the first ordinary selector anyone adds to the stylesheet, 'h1:not(.foo) { ... }', makes the suite fail with 'the cascade guard cannot read the selector', so the vocabulary will have to be widened in a hurry the first time it bites. That is the maintenance bill, stated honestly rather than as an argument for deleting it.

review.title: The work order states a property of the delivered file that this diff does not have. Approach §'After all of this' says: 'the literal 'page-title' appears in the test file only inside the H1_HOOK matcher comment and the shipped-markup sample strings at lines 146-152.' In the file as merged the literal appears in eight further places, and one of them is load-bearing for how the guard reads: line 1567 hardcodes `const cls = 'page-title';` at the head of the resolver-pinning test, and lines 1572, 1580, 1582, 1596, 1599 and 1605 build their selectors from it. The functional consequence is small — a coordinated rename of .page-title to .pageHeading is still green, because the pinning test supplies its own cls and never reads the markup or the stylesheet, which is what AC-3 asks for. The design consequence is not small: the test that is supposed to be the guard's ground truth is now written against a name the rest of the file has deliberately stopped knowing, so it cannot detect a break in the class plumbing no matter how the class is renamed, and the file carries a claim about its own contents that is simply untrue. A reader checking the work order's promise against the file will find it broken and stop trusting the rest of the order.
